claims.text: Six hours of high-energy ball milling of CoCrFeNiTi powders induces severe lattice strain.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling refines the CoCrFeNiTi powder to a nanocrystalline grain size.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the thermodynamic or activation-energy barrier for a metastable FCC/BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C under uniaxial pressure densifies the milled CoCrFeNiTi powder.
At 1000°C, SPS can avoid excessive Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the stability of the proposed FCC/BCC transition in CoCrFeNiTi.
The defect density and lattice distortion introduced by six-hour milling increase the configurational-entropy contribution to Gibbs free energy.
The milling-induced change in configurational entropy stabilizes an FCC/BCC solid solution.
The high strain energy of the milled state kinetically traps the solid solution during SPS.
Longer milling produces finer grains in the SPS-consolidated bulk and raises hardness through Hall–Petch strengthening.
Powder-metallurgy processing can produce a finer-grained bulk material than an arc-melted counterpart.
The proposed process will produce fully dense CoCrFeNiTi.
The processed alloy will have high Vickers hardness.
The processed alloy will exhibit a dominant FCC/BCC solid-solution phase with negligible HCP precipitation.
The processed alloy will have minimal porosity.
Arc-melted CoCrFeNiTi has coarse dendritic structures and severe compositional segregation.
Arc-melted CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and inherent porosity.
Temperatures significantly above 1000°C can cause Ti-induced HCP precipitation or decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
Temperatures significantly above 1000°C can cause excessive grain growth that negates grain-boundary strengthening.
Vickers hardness testing at a 100 g load isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The boundary says temperatures above 1000°C promote Ti-driven HCP precipitation, whereas the falsification rule interprets HCP at 1000°C as evidence that the temperature was insufficient to stabilize the solid solution. These imply opposite temperature dependences for HCP formation.

The hypothesis invokes a 'single-phase stability window,' while the mechanism and predicted outcome repeatedly describe an FCC/BCC solid solution or mixed FCC/BCC state. It is unclear whether the intended product is a single FCC or BCC phase, a dual-phase FCC+BCC material, or a transition between them.
